title: Layer 4 vs Layer 7 Load Balancing
description: Understand the differences between transport-layer and application-layer load balancing, including trade-offs, use cases, and real-world deployment patterns.

data.text: Load balancers operate at different layers of the OSI model. Layer 4 load balancers make routing decisions based on IP addresses and port numbers, while Layer 7 load balancers inspect the actual application payload, such as HTTP headers or URLs. Understanding when to use each approach is fundamental to designing scalable systems.

A Layer 4 load balancer works at the transport layer. It sees source and destination IP addresses and ports, but cannot see inside the packet. Common implementations include Network Load Balancers on AWS and IPVS in Kubernetes. Because it does not parse application data, it operates with very low latency and can handle millions of requests per second.

data.title: Key Trait
data.text: L4 load balancers route based on IP/port only. They do not inspect HTTP methods, headers, or body content.

A Layer 7 load balancer operates at the application layer. It understands protocols such as HTTP, HTTPS, and gRPC. This enables path-based routing, header rewriting, cookie-based session affinity, and TLS termination. Examples include NGINX, HAProxy in HTTP mode, and cloud application load balancers.

data.title: Interview Tip
data.text: When asked which layer to use, start with requirements: Do you need path-based routing or TLS termination? If yes, L7 is likely correct. If you only need raw throughput, L4 may be sufficient.

data.title: Takeaway
points: Layer 4 load balancers route by IP and port with minimal overhead.
Layer 7 load balancers inspect application data for smarter routing.
Choose L4 for throughput and L7 for protocol-aware features.
data.takeaway: The right choice depends on whether you need application-layer visibility or raw forwarding performance.
